summary: Summation No. 31 covers April 1948 (statistics mostly for February-March). Politically, government employees' unions accepted the 2,920-yen wage scale on 16 April after SCAP forbade a communications strike; the Ashida coalition was strained by the Social Democratic demand to suspend war bond interest, cabinet disagreement over labor law revision, and the Tsuji hoarded-goods inquiry. Korean protests against school closures in Osaka and Kobe required Occupation troops. The Diet created the Maritime Safety Board and restored parliamentary vice-ministers; the purge continued and the IMTFE heard final defense summations. Economically, March output hit postwar highs in steel, chemicals, rayon, cotton and silk fabrics, with coal at 2.86 million tons, while the February trade deficit was $60.9 million. Finance, rationing, labor, health, education and media statistics follow. Historians will find detailed tables on production, trade, repatriation and the war crimes trials.
highlights: Government unions accepted the 2,920-yen wage scale 16 April after SCAP barred a communications workers' general strike.
Social Democrats' proposal to suspend war bond interest split the coalition; the council reported both sides.
Koreans protested school closures in Osaka and Kobe 23-26 April; Occupation troops restored order in Kobe.
Maritime Safety Authorities Bill passed 15 April, authorizing up to 10,000 men and 125 vessels.
IMTFE defense summations completed 15 April; the court adjourned 16 April to prepare judgment on 25 accused.
February trade deficit was $60.9 million; 73 percent of imports came from the United States.
By 17 April 711,036 persons were screened in the purge; 4,880 removed and 2,876 barred.
764,900 persons were still awaiting repatriation to Japan; 396 returned in April.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of Summation No. 31 (April 1948), a table of contents for Parts I to IV (General, Political, Economic, Social) and a list of charts, maps and graphs, from the industrial production indexes through coal, textiles, finance, health and publishing tables to the Map of Japan.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Brief digest of the month's developments across all fields, paragraph-numbered.

sections.title: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: The Restitution Advisory Committee was established 13 April to advise the Supreme Commander on disposing of looted property found in Japan. The Civil Property Custodian chairs it ex officio, with one representative from each Reparations and Restitution Delegation of the 11 Far Eastern Commission nations wishing to take part.

sections.title: Political Activities
sections.summary: Government employees accepted the 2,920-yen wage scale; Cabinet members disagreed on labor-law changes; the war bond interest dispute went to interparty talks; and the Cabinet failed to settle the 1948-49 budget. Also covered: Tsuji fund inquiry, party maneuvers, 18 bills, purge totals, Korean school protests in Osaka and Kobe, the Maritime Safety bill and war crimes trial.

sections.title: Economic Activities
sections.summary: March output rose in coal, pig iron, steel, chemicals (record caustic soda), machinery, textiles, bicycles (47,120) and motor vehicles. February imports were $70.3 million against exports of $9.4 million, a deficit of $60.9 million. Also: new radio and telegraph links, the 220.4 billion yen note circulation, 353 looted ships, 7,805 machine tools shipped as reparations, and scientific research notes.

sections.title: Social Activities
sections.summary: Japanese B encephalitis research began at the National Institute of Health, penicillin output rose 138 percent, and 764,900 persons awaited repatriation. Education items: 647 million yen for lower secondary schools, 94,650,553 textbooks authorized, and the National Diet Library moved. Religion, art exhibition, public opinion surveys, radio, films and music are also noted.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Government and politics, public safety, and legal affairs and war crimes.

sections.title: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Resolution of the government-employee wage dispute, war bond interest controversy, Tsuji hoarded-goods inquiry, party positions, Diet business and the purge.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: The government employees' dispute over the 2,920-yen scale ended 16 April after SCAP three times barred communications strikes; Ashida and Labor Minister Kato clashed over labor-law revision. Also: the war bond interest conference, Ashida's and Kitamura's economic statements, provisional budgets, the governors' conference, Local Autonomy Law amendment, Tsuji inquiry, bribery arrests including Vice-minister Ino, and a national inventory of hoarded goods.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: The Democratic Party defined 'modified capitalism', stayed optimistic about the coalition, and denied merger with the Democratic Liberals, losing three members to them. Social Democrats defended war bond interest suspension, the Satsuki-kai backed Kato, and the party gained to 123 lower house seats. Democratic Liberals attacked the Cabinet; the People's Cooperative Party backed it.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: SCAP urged curbs on Diet absenteeism and the House cancelled its recess. Ashida asked to extend the session to end of May. The Diet received 17 bills and enacted 18 laws including the Coal Board and Maritime Safety bills. Democratic and People's Cooperative candidates won the Hiroshima by-election, and 22 parliamentary vice-ministers were appointed 15 April.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: By 17 April 711,036 persons were screened, with 4,880 removed and 2,876 barred; 189,162 were finally designated. Media screening reached 490 final designations, with 78 pending and 331 writers provisionally designated. The Appeals Board rejected 135 appeals. Destroyed records were being replaced, and the Special Investigation Bureau was organized on 20 April with nine regional headquarters.

sections.title: Public Safety
sections.summary: Korean-school closure protests in Osaka (23-26 April) left 23 Koreans and 58 police injured and 183 arrested; Occupation Forces helped disperse Kobe crowds that held Hyogo officials captive. February saw 149,885 offenses and 79,220 arrests. Rural Police crime laboratory funded, Maritime Safety Authorities Bill passed, prison population 87,233, 548 rail accidents, 1,806 fires.

sections.title: Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The Supreme Court upheld capital punishment on 12 March and a High Marine Court of Inquiry opened 1 April. Atrocity investigations on hand fell to 972; 610 war criminals tried by 20 April (572 convicted, 94 sentenced to death). At the IMTFE the defense summations for all 25 accused (Minami through Umezu) were completed 15 April and the court adjourned 16 April to prepare judgment.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Thirteen sections of statistics and narrative on production, trade, labor, prices, finance, property and science.

sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Land sales to tenants reached 146,558 cho in March (427,320 cumulative), and 12,051 agricultural cooperatives finished preliminary meetings. Reclamation reached 294,522.7 hectares since 1945, with 499,725 families receiving land. February marine production totaled 110,464 tons; fishing petroleum allocations mostly fell in April. Antarctic whaling yielded 17,544.6 long tons of whale oil; whale oil shipments went to Bremen.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: March log production rose to 88,984,500 cubic feet, and February firewood and charcoal output increased. About 2,865,884 cho needed reforestation, with seed supply 22,768 kilograms short, and 1947 cutting outran replanting (866,170 against 430,810 cho). March coal output was 2,862,500 tons, with 29,330,000 tons for the fiscal year; coal mine employees numbered 516,897. March crude oil was 16,016 kiloliters.

sections.title: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: March coke output was 221,910 tons. Steel mills set postwar records: pig iron 44,777 tons and rolled steel 76,927 tons. Copper, zinc, lead and ferroalloys rose, aluminum fell to 374 tons, and cement reached 131,669 tons. Chemicals hit new highs (ammonium sulfate 66,186 tons, superphosphate 81,486). Machine tools numbered 327; locomotives and rolling stock increased.

sections.title: Manufacturing
sections.summary: February flour output jumped 290 percent to 103,066 tons after larger wheat releases; sake peaked at 80,780 hectoliters while tobacco output fell. March pulp rose 10 percent and paper reached 34,492 tons. Trucks fell to 942 chassis, three-wheelers hit a postwar high of 1,093, and bicycles a record 47,120. Leather, agricultural implements, handicrafts, business machines, matches and timepieces also reported.

sections.title: Textile Industries
sections.summary: March textile output rose generally, with postwar peaks in rayon filament, spun rayon, cotton and silk fabrics. Cotton yarn reached 23,181,000 pounds, the highest since July 1947, and cotton cloth topped 65.7 million square yards, mostly for export. Raw silk gained 1,236 bales to 10,106; first postwar acetate yarn, acetone and wood pulp imports arrived; wool, bast fiber, knit goods, clothing and dyeing figures also reported. Opening pages cover sewing machines (12,272 home units), cosmetics and toys.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered commercial vehicles rose to 163,766, of which 67.5 percent were operable; deadlined trucks lacked fuel, tires or repairs. Government railways carried 303,921,713 passengers, up 9.5 percent, and freight reached 9,861,800 metric tons. Coastal steel-ship cargo was 955,100 tons. Electric generation was 2,607,867,000 kilowatt hours, up 17 percent, and gas output was 61,338,471 cubic meters. Coal allocation plans for 1948 are described.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: Telephones in service rose 1.3 percent to 1,195,238, and new radiotelephone and radiotelegraph links opened to Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Netherlands East Indies. Radio households reached 6,443,206, and a school survey found 87 percent of primary schools equipped. Mail volumes, postal savings restoration, vehicles and building projects are reported. Vacuum tube output hit a postwar high; absenteeism was 4.9 percent; a Diet appropriation of ¥3,289,493,000 and a White Paper projecting a deficit over ¥5.3 billion are noted.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: The Government resisted revising labor laws as the government workers' dispute ended 16 April with acceptance of the ¥2,920 wage level and a 15-grade pay classification plan. Other settlements covered coal miners, metal miners, private railways, textiles and Toho Studio, while seamen and Tokyo Shibaura talks continued. Unions numbered 29,378 with 6,243,017 members. Also covered are Economic Reconstruction Council dissolution, workmen's compensation, labor supply bans and unemployment insurance, February disputes involving 189,558 workers, and labor education.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: February imports were estimated at $70,261,684 and exports at $9,400,019, leaving a deficit of about $60.9 million. About 73 percent of imports came from the United States, with India and Cuba also major sources. Foodstuffs were 44 percent and textiles, chiefly raw cotton, 41 percent of imports. Textiles were 41 percent of exports, followed by nonmetallic minerals and foodstuffs. Private contracts approved were 34 import and 604 export contracts.

sections.title: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Full April rations were met from carryover stocks after 1947 crop quotas were fulfilled in March (rice 100.1 percent), and the substitute-rice program ended. Fish prices were revised, soybean flour and copra meal released, and incentive goods to rice farmers nearly delivered. February rents, family expenditures (6,214 yen) and consumer prices rose; railway food losses and 6,646 enforcement cases were reported.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes outstanding reached 220.44 billion yen on 30 April, while government securities held fell 6.7 billion yen. Reconstruction Finance Bank loans stood at 59.46 billion yen, with mining and electric power taking most new lending. Also covered: securities liquidation, insurance account mergers, the new Securities and Exchange Law, 134 control organizations closed in March, 1947-48 tax receipts of 124.9 billion yen, April provisional budgets, a 360.8 billion yen national debt and local government finance.

sections.title: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property worth 3.76 million yen was newly taken into custody, with restitutions to the Netherlands, China and Britain; 353 looted ships were reported, 55 percent sunk. The SCAP Custody Account reached 265.2 million yen. SCAP approved 282 restricted-concern transactions, 73 control organizations were ordered closed, 325 concerns designated for reorganization, and Fair Trade Commission filings continued. Advance reparations shipments reached 7,805 machine tools by April.

sections.title: Science and Technology
sections.summary: The Renewal Committee for the Organization of Science held its eighth and final meeting on 25-27 March, recommending a Science Council under the Prime Minister's office and a Cabinet-level coordinating committee. Society meetings, research on a polyvinyl alcohol fiber at Kyoto, and Honda's Comet were reported. Japanese Standards in effect reached 1,009 (1,956 of all types); 175 patents were granted; terminology standards for 20,810 terms were decided, and new publications appeared.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health and welfare; education, religion, cultural resources and media of expression.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: About 36.4 million typhoid inoculations had been given by 26 April; a 98-case typhus outbreak at an Osaka hospital was contained, and March communicable disease figures were given. Medical supply production and distribution were tabulated, with penicillin at a record 157,019 vials. Welfare aid reached 3,077,031 persons; LARA shipments, Red Cross decisions, 396 repatriates in April (5,843,095 total) and February vital statistics followed.

sections.title: Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: April 1948: ¥647 million supplementary budget for lower secondary schools, glass and cement allocations, Korean school protests at Kobe, 12,123 new lower secondary schools reported, textbook authorization committee and 94.7 million textbooks authorized. Religion and cultural items follow. Public opinion surveys (coeducation, Central Screening Committee, tax revision), information programs, press comment, radio, films, and a Fukuoka SCAP library close the section.
